interactions.summary: The degree-critique block turns into a short exchange about how American workplaces now expect instant readiness instead of training, reinforcing the loss of apprenticeship.

Jiang argues that medicine proves mentorship matters more than sorting by brilliance: he says China gets acceptable doctors through long apprenticeship while America wastes top students inside a bloated parasitic system.
Greg extends Jiang's point by linking mentorship decline, Chinese medicine, and Harvard's endowment logic, then restates the venture-capital metaphor as a marketing machine for elite schools.
Greg pivots from institutional critique to prophecy, asking whether Jiang holds more extreme predictions than the ones he has already published and whether some are too explosive to say publicly.

claims.claim: Greg says American workplaces increasingly refuse to train people and instead expect workers to arrive fully formed, which creates inefficiency.
claims.temporal_scope: Current labor-system diagnosis made by the host on 2025-10-07.

claims.claim: Jiang says China staffs medicine with weaker students but compensates through years of mentorship, internship, and guided experience.
claims.temporal_scope: Comparative institutional claim made on 2025-10-07 about present-day China.

claims.claim: Jiang says the American medical system is bloated, expensive, parasitical, and unjust despite being staffed by top students.
Jiang says most jobs do not require passing through meritocratic tournaments; they require proper mentoring and apprenticeship, which would reopen access to the American dream.
claims.temporal_scope: Normative labor and education claim made on 2025-10-07.

claims.claim: Greg says alternative-minded Americans often look to older Chinese healing traditions for wisdom even while modern Chinese manufacturing is implicated in pharmaceutical harms.
Greg says Harvard's huge endowment and selective winner-making create the public perception that elite success in America is impossible without passing through a small set of schools.
Greg says forecasters in troubled times need unusual courage because power punishes people who openly predict imperial collapse.
Greg asks whether Jiang has additional predictions too extreme to publish publicly even after Jiang's recent viral success.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang's anti-meritocracy line sharpens into a labor model: what most work needs is not genius selection but long apprenticeship.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it requires you to be mentored and apprenticed
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the constructive half of his education critique and gives the read a positive alternative to elite sorting.

signature_moments.moment: Greg turns Harvard into a branding engine that teaches ordinary people elite success only comes through five anointed schools.
signature_moments.source_phrase: successful people go to these five schools
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows how institutional prestige becomes mass psychological discipline, not just elite selection.

signature_moments.moment: The Hari Seldon comparison reframes Jiang as a collapse forecaster speaking under imperial pressure.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there's a certain courage in forecasting
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It marks the thematic turn from credentialism to prophecy and sets up the interview's most extreme prediction block.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Greg names this as a social form that has eroded in America, aligning with Jiang's case for apprenticeship over credential sorting.
Jiang's preferred model for training people into competence, contrasted with meritocratic gatekeeping and degree inflation.
Greg's Foundation reference for a figure who predicts imperial collapse and is punished by power for saying it out loud.

chronology_notes.note: This packet closes the credentialism block and opens the interview's prophetic section with a direct invitation for Jiang to disclose predictions he has withheld until now.

uncertainty_notes.note: Some medical-system phrasing is ASR-garbled and Greg's China-pharma detour is loose, but the packet's core contrast between apprenticeship and meritocratic sorting is clear.
